sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own generations by matching the teacher's token probabilities. These probabilities entangle two kinds of information: which tokens the teacher prefers, and how confident it is. The latter reflects the teacher's own capacity and calibration, which a smaller student may be unable to reproduce. Because the teacher temperature changes these values without changing the ordering, OPD is also sensitive to the temperature choice. We ask whether the teacher's ordering of candidate tokens is enough, and propose Order-Only On-Policy Distillation (O$^{3}$PD). At each student-generated prefix, O$^{3}$PD trains the student to reproduce the order of the teacher's top-$K$ tokens, without fitting their probability values. The objective is therefore invariant to the teacher temperature and needs no temperature tuning. Across six teacher--student pairs, O$^{3}$PD outperforms OPD on the average over HMMT25, AIME24, and AIME25 in every pair, by up to 2.9 points, with gains of up to 5.6 points on AIME25. Other ranking losses yield similar gains, so the benefit comes from ordinal supervision itself. Analysis shows that O$^{3}$PD departs further from the teacher's probabilities than OPD, yet reproduces its ranking more faithfully and yields a stronger student. The ranking, not the probability values, thus carries the knowledge that on-policy distillation needs to transfer.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Knowledge distillation (KD) transfers the capabilities of strong teacher model to weaker student. Hinton et al. (2015) showed that the teachers full output distribution, rather than single hard label, is what makes this transfer effective: the probabilities assigned to competing outputs encode relationships that hard label cannot express. This insight made distribution matching the default recipe for distillation. The student is trained to reproduce not only which output the teacher prefers, but also the exact probability that the teacher assigns to every alternative. For autoregressive language models, the contexts in which supervision is given matter as much as the supervision itself. Sequence-level distillation trains the student with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on teachergenerated responses (Kim & Rush, 2016). This recipe has two weaknesses. Each position supplies single target token, so the teachers preferences over alternatives are lost. In addition, the student is trained on teacher-generated prefixes but generates from its own prefixes at inference time, so its errors lead it into contexts it has never been trained on. On-policy distillation (OPD) removes this mismatch by querying the teacher on student-generated trajectories and training the student to match the teachers token distribution at the states it actually visits (Gu Figure 1: (a) Three nested levels of teacher supervision. (b) The corresponding objectives.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024). OPD has since become standard approach for distilling reasoning models (Yang et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026). Matching probabilities, however, asks the student for more than it needs. The teachers probability values mix two kinds of information: which tokens it prefers, and how confident it is in that preference. The first is what the student must acquire to reason like the teacher. The second reflects the teachers own capacity and calibration, which much smaller student may be unable to reproduce (Cho & Hariharan, 2019; Mirzadeh et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2024). distribution-matching objective penalizes every deviation from these values, so the student spends much of its capacity fitting confidence profile that it cannot reach. The problem shows up clearly in practice. OPD is highly sensitive to the teachers logit temperature, and the best temperature differs from one teacherstudent pair to another (Figure 7). Moreover, OPD can degrade the student as training continues, falling below the base model it started from (Figure 3). These observations raise basic question: does on-policy distillation need the teachers probabilities at all, or is the teachers ordering of candidate tokens enough? We answer this question by separating three nested levels of teacher supervision: token choice, token ranking, and token probabilities (Figure 1a). sampled target reveals single choice. ranked candidate list reveals which tokens the teacher considers plausible and in what order it prefers them. probability distribution additionally fixes numerical confidence for each token. Existing objectives occupy the two ends of this hierarchy (Figure 1b). Sequence KD imitates only the realized token, while logit KD, including distribution-matching OPD, matches the full probability distribution. Soft-target distillation shows that information about alternatives matters, but it does not show that their exact probabilities must be transferred. We argue that the middle level, namely the teachers ranking, carries the knowledge that matters for distillation, and that the remaining probability values act as constraint rather than signal. Building on this view, we propose Order-Only On-Policy Distillation (O3PD). At each studentgenerated prefix, the teacher selects its top-K tokens and orders them by probability. The student is then trained with an adjacent logistic ranking loss, which requires each candidate to score higher than the next one in the teachers order. The teachers probabilities decide which candidates are selected and how they are ordered, but their values never enter the loss. The 1 adjacent constraints determine the complete ranking through transitivity, so O3PD transfers the full teacher order with minimal set of constraints while leaving the student free to set its own probability values. Because dividing logits by positive temperature does not change their order, O3PD is invariant to the teacher temperature by construction and needs no temperature tuning. Ordinal and relational supervision have been studied in classification distillation and in learning to rank (Huang et al., 2022; Reddi et al., 2021; Guan et al., 2025; Li & Cheng, 2026; Bassam et al., 2025), but typically alongside KL terms or confidence weights, and over fixed label sets with ground-truth labels. O3PD uses the teachers order as its only signal and applies it to on-policy distillation of autoregressive models, where the candidate list is rebuilt by the teacher at every student-generated prefix. We evaluate O3PD on six Qwen3 teacherstudent configurations and three competition-level mathematics benchmarks: HMMT25, AIME24, and AIME25. Against an OPD baseline, O3PD improves the three-benchmark average in all six configurations, by up to 2.9 points. It improves AIME25 in every configuration, by as much as 5.6 points, and it outperforms SFT and GRPO at every student scale. O3PD also trains stably: while OPD peaks early and then declines, O3PD keeps improving until the end of training. Our analysis explains where these gains come from. O3PD agrees less with the teachers probability values than OPD does, yet it reproduces the teachers token ordering and candidate set more faithfully. It also moves the student much further from its initialization, most strongly for the smallest student, which is also the student that gains the most. Probability matching thus holds the student close to its starting point, whereas ordinal supervision lets the student reshape its distribution in the direction the teachers preferences indicate. Our contributions are as follows: We identify probability matching as an unnecessary constraint in on-policy distillation. We separate the teachers token ordering from its probability values and show that the ordering alone provides stronger training signal. We introduce O3PD, which trains the student to reproduce the teachers top-K token order, by default through adjacent pairwise constraints. O3PD is invariant to the teacher

We show that O3PD outperforms OPD on the three-benchmark average in all six teacher student configurations and exceeds SFT and GRPO in every configuration. Through analysis, we show that O3PD learns the teachers ranking rather than its probabilities, and that it allows the smallest student to move substantially further from its initialization.

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Knowledge distillation (KD) can be characterized along two largely orthogonal axes: where supervision is applied (the prefix states on which the student is trained) and what teacher information is transferred at each state.

sections.title: 2.1 LLM DISTILLATION: FROM TEACHER STATES TO STUDENT STATES
sections.content: Early LLM distillation trains the student on fixed sequences. Sequence-level distillation uses teacher-generated responses as targets (Kim & Rush, 2016), optionally enriched with rationales (Hsieh et al., 2023) or organized as preferences (Zhang et al., 2025), while white-box variants match the teachers token distributions along such sequences (Hinton et al., 2015; Kim & Rush, 2016). In both cases, the student is supervised on teacheror data-induced prefixes, whereas at inference it conditions on its own generations, creating traininference mismatch. On-policy methods mitigate this mismatch by querying the teacher on student-generated states, minimizing reverse KL (Gu et al., 2024), generalized divergences (Agarwal et al., 2024), or skewed divergences with adaptive replay (Ko et al., 2024). Training on student states, however, introduces new difficulty: when student trajectories are of low quality, teacher supervision on them becomes less reliable. SWITCH therefore lets the teacher intervene in generation when teacherstudent discrepancies grow (Koo et al., 2025), and SKD replaces student tokens that fall outside the teachers top-K (Xu et al., 2025); in SKD, the teachers ranking decides which tokens enter the trajectory, but the training objective remains distribution matching. Complementary work improves efficiency through difficulty-aware sample selection (He et al., 2025) and curricula (Zhang & Liu, 2025). Across these methods, what changes is the states, the divergence, the trajectory construction, or the data schedule; the per-state target remains the teachers probability distribution. O3PD keeps on-policy states but replaces this target with the teachers top-K ranking. 2.2 DISTILLATION BEYOND PROBABILITY MATCHING Matching the teachers distribution requires the student to reproduce not only which candidates the teacher prefers but also how confident the teacher is. Relaxations of this target can be characterized by the transformations of teacher scores that leave the target unchanged. KL is invariant only to logit shifts. Logit Standardization (Sun et al., 2024) and DIST (Huang et al., 2022) additionally remove scale and are invariant to affine transformations, but still consume continuous scores: nonlinear yet order-preserving re-scoring of the teacher changes their targets. purely ordinal target is invariant to all strictly monotone transformations and transfers the teachers preferences without its confidence. Ranking-based methods move toward such ordinal targets but differ from O3PD in either the signal or the setting. On the signal side, RKKD adds Kendalls τ loss as an auxiliary to KL, so teacher probabilities still enter the objective (Guan et al., 2025), and PLD, PlackettLuce loss akin to ListMLE (Xia et al., 2008), weights each ranked choice by teacher confidence (Bassam et al., 2025). On the setting side, these methods, as well as OPKDs pairwise ordering objectives (Li & Cheng, 2026), are designed for classification over fixed label set with ground-truth labels, and RankDistil and DGR for ranking fixed pools of items or passages (Reddi et al., 2021; Li et al., 2024); at studentgenerated decoding states, by contrast, the candidate set changes from state to state and no groundtruth token exists. Conversely, BiLD operates in LLM distillation and restricts supervision to the teachers top-K logits, but matches their pairwise differences, which are shiftbut not scale-invariant and thus still encode preference strength (Li et al., 2025). O3PD satisfies both requirements: at each student-generated state, it keeps only the identities and order of the teachers top-K tokens.

sections.title: 3 ORDER-ONLY ON-POLICY DISTILLATION
sections.content: Knowledge distillation can transfer different forms of teacher supervision, from generated sequences to token-level probability distributions. We study an intermediate choice: transferring the teachers candidate tokens and their relative ordering without fitting the teachers probability magnitudes. We instantiate this choice as Order-Only On-Policy Distillation (O3PD), which learns from teacher rankings on student-generated contexts. 3.1 FROM SEQUENCE AND DISTRIBUTION TARGETS TO ORDINAL SUPERVISION transfers Sequence-level knowledge distillation (Sequence KD) teachergenerated responses. Given prompt and teacher response yT , the student minimizes knowledge through Lseq(x, yT ) = 1 yT t=1 yT (cid:88) log πθ(yT x, yT <t). Table 1: Comparison of KD methods. Method Sequence KD OPD O3PD On-policy Temperature invariant Magnitudefree (1) This objective trains the student to reproduce the teachers generations, but represents supervision as selected token at each prefix without explicitly retaining preferences among alternative candidates. Moreover, training follows teacher-generated prefixes rather than output from the current student. On-policy distillation (OPD) instead obtains teacher supervision on student-generated contexts. The student samples responses from its current policy, and the teacher provides predictive distributions at the resulting prefixes. representative distribution-matching objective is LOPD(s) = JSD(cid:0)pT K( s) πθ,K( s)(cid:1), (2) This supervision preserves the teachers judgments over multiple candidates, but couples their relative ordering with the strength of their assigned probabilities. Even when candidate rankings remain unchanged, different probability assignments yield different training signals. Changing the teacher temperature likewise changes the target distribution while preserving its ordering, introducing an additional temperature-selection problem. When teacher and student differ substantially in reasoning behavior or capability, the teachers probability assignments may also be difficult for the student to reproduce, complicating knowledge transfer. This motivates question: can we transfer the teachers preferences without requiring matching their probability magnitudes? O3PD separates these two forms of information. At each student-generated prefix, we extract the teachers top-K candidates and their ordering, then train the student through adjacent comparisons. The candidate set determines which tokens are compared, and the ordering determines the preferred direction; teacher probability magnitudes are not fitting targets. This design has three properties.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: First, it retains on-policy training, providing supervision on contexts encountered by the current student. Second, it yields teacher-temperature invariant supervision: at fixed context, positive temperature scaling preserves the candidate set and its ordering, leaving the O3PD objective unchanged. This removes the need to select teacher temperature. More generally, because the objective depends on the teacher only through its top-K ordering, it is invariant to any strictly increasing transformation of the teachers scores at each context, of which temperature scaling is special case. Finally, it provides magnitude-free supervision: the objective specifies which candidate should be preferred but prescribes no target for how strongly, so the student is never required to reproduce the teachers probability gaps. Table 1 summarizes the comparison.

Logistic and Top-Weighted Logistic keep the BradleyTerry loss (Bradley & Terry, 1952) and change only the comparison set. Logistic supervises all K(K 1)/2 pairs, directly penalizing coarse violations such as the first candidate against the last, which the adjacent loss constrains only through transitivity. Top-Weighted Logistic weights each pair by the reciprocal rank of its preferred candidate, concentrating supervision on the head of the list, which matters most for decoding. ListMLE instead imposes the order as whole: under the PlackettLuce model (Plackett, 1975; Luce, 2005), it treats the ranking as sequence of choices, each selecting the next candidate from those not yet ranked. Since PlackettLuce reduces to BradleyTerry on any two candidates, ListMLE expresses the same preferences as O3PD, but over the full list at once. The choice among these objectives therefore determines how the order is imposed, not what is transferred.

sections.title: 4.1 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: Models and data. We distill within the Qwen3 family (Yang et al., 2025). Each student (1.7B, 4B, or 8B) is paired with every larger teacher (4B, 8B, or 14B), giving six teacherstudent configurations. The teacher is kept frozen, and all methods are trained on the mathematical reasoning subset of OpenThoughts (Guha et al., 2026). Full training details are given in Appendix A. Evaluation. We evaluate on three competition-level benchmarks, HMMT25, AIME24, and AIME25, and report Avg@12: the accuracy of the final answer averaged over 12 sampled responses per problem, drawn as four samples under each of three seeds. Average denotes the unweighted mean over the three benchmarks, and all differences are reported in absolute points. For OPD and O3PD, we evaluate every 20 training steps and report the checkpoint with the highest Average. This selection can only favor method whose performance declines during training. For the 8B1.7B pair, OPD peaks early and then degrades while O3PD keeps improving (Figure 3), so comparing final checkpoints instead would widen the gap in favor of O3PD. Baselines. We compare O3PD with the base student, SFT, GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), and OPD (Gu et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024). SFT and GRPO results are taken from Zhao et al. (2026), which uses the same student models, training data, and evaluation protocol. OPD is our primary baseline and is trained under exactly the same configurations as O3PD. It minimizes the JensenShannon divergence between the student and teacher distributions restricted to the teachers top-K tokens, with = 8 and teacher temperature = 1, so that both methods see the same candidate set at every prefix and differ only in whether the probability values enter the loss. 4.2 MAIN RESULTS O3PD consistently outperforms baselines. Table 3 shows that O3PD achieves higher average than OPD in all six configurations. The gain is modest for the 8B student (+0.6) and larger for the smaller students: +2.3 and +1.9 for the 4B student (14B and 8B teachers), and +2.6 and +2.9 for the 1.7B student with the 8B and 4B teachers. The exception is the 14B1.7B pair, which improves by only 0.3, suggesting that when the capacity gap is largest, even the teachers ranking becomes harder for the student to reproduce. The gains concentrate on AIME. O3PD improves AIME25 in every configuration, by 3.4 points on average and up to 5.6. It also gives the largest single gain in the table, +6.4 on AIME24 for 4B1.7B. Overall, O3PD improves over OPD in 14 of the 18 comparisons. O3PD also exceeds the base model, SFT, and GRPO in average score in every configuration. For the 1.7B student, for example, it reaches 40.9, compared with 37.7 for GRPO and 35.8 for SFT. SFT falls below the base model at every scale, which highlights the value of on-policy supervision. O3PD improves steadily throughout training. Figure 3 tracks both methods for the 8B1.7B pair. OPD peaks at step 20 (38.1) and then declines below the base student (37.7). O3PD instead keeps improving and reaches its best mean (40.7) at the final step. The contrast is sharpest on AIME25, where O3PD climbs from 35.6 to 43.1 while OPD falls back to its starting point. Ranking objective. Besides Adjacent Logistic, we evaluate the Logistic, Top-Weighted Logistic, and ListMLE variants of O3PD. All variants outperform OPD at = 8, by 1.3 to 2.6 points, so ordinal supervision is robust to the choice of ranking loss. Adjacent Logistic and ListMLE perform best, within 0.1 points of each other, even though Adjacent Logistic supervises only 7 of the 28 pairs used by Logistic. By transitivity, the adjacent relations already fix the full ranking, so supervising the remaining pairs brings no further gain. We use Adjacent Logistic by default, as it matches the best result with the fewest constraints.

sections.title: 5 ANALYSIS
sections.content: Section 4.2 shows that O3PD produces stronger students than OPD and, on the 8B1.7B pair, keeps improving where OPD degrades. We now examine where this advantage comes from. We first ask what the student acquires from the teacher under ordinal supervision (Section 5.1), and then how training reshapes the student relative to its initialization (Section 5.2). 5.1 LEARNING THE TEACHERS ORDER, NOT ITS PROBABILITIES We measure token-level agreement between the student and the teacher on student-generated responses for the 8B1.7B pair (Figure 5). At each position t, let denote the top-8 tokens of the teacher and the student. JSD@Top-8 is the JensenShannon divergence between the two distributions restricted to and renormalized, and measures how closely the student reproduces the teachers probability values. Kendalls τ compares the orderings that the two models induce on /8 measures whether the student considers the same candidates plausible. Top-1 agreement is the fraction of positions at which the two models share the most likely token, and student entropy is the entropy of the students next-token distribution over the full vocabulary. All metrics are averaged over positions. , and top-8 overlap t and The first metric concerns probability values. OPD behaves as its objective prescribes and keeps the JSD to the teacher low throughout training. The JSD of O3PD is consistently higher and grows as training proceeds, which is expected since O3PD never asks the student to match the teachers probability values. On ordering and candidate set, the relation reverses. O3PD achieves

From left to right: JSD@Top-8, Kendalls τ , top-8 overlap, top-1 agreement, and student entropy. O3PD departs further from the teachers probabilities than OPD, yet agrees more closely with its ordering and candidate set, and maintains higher entropy throughout training. higher Kendalls τ than OPD for most of training and ends clearly above it, and its top-8 overlap stays above that of OPD at nearly every evaluation, while top-1 agreement is comparable. O3PD thus transfers the structure that governs generation, namely which candidates the teacher considers plausible and how it orders them, and leaves the probability values free. The student also keeps broader distribution: its entropy stays above that of OPD throughout training, whereas probability matching pulls the student toward the teachers confidence profile. Together with Figure 3, these results show that closer probability matching does not translate into better reasoning: OPD attains the lower JSD, yet O3PD attains the higher accuracy. 5.2 RESHAPING THE STUDENT Figure 4 places each checkpoint according to its distance from the base student and its distance from the teacher. For every student size, O3PD checkpoints sit further from the teachers probabilities than OPD checkpoints, consistent with Section 5.1. How far the student moves from its initialization, however, depends on student size. For the 1.7B student, OPD checkpoints stay close to the base student, whereas O3PD checkpoints move several times further away. For the 4B student, the two methods move comparable distances, and for the 8B student, OPD moves further than O3PD. Ordinal supervision thus does not uniformly produce larger updates; it produces them for the smallest student, where matching the teachers probabilities is hardest. The mechanism is intuitive. small student cannot reproduce the probability values of much larger teacher, so magnitude-matching objective spends much of its capacity on target that the student cannot reach. Ordinal supervision removes this constraint. The student is free to restructure its own distribution, provided that it preserves the teachers ordering of the candidates, and the smallest student makes the most use of this freedom.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented Order-Only On-Policy Distillation (O3PD), which trains the student to reproduce the teachers top-K token ranking without matching the teachers probability values. Because the supervision depends only on the teachers order, O3PD is invariant to the teacher temperature and requires no temperature tuning. Across six Qwen3 teacherstudent configurations, O3PD outperforms OPD on the three-benchmark average in every configuration, also exceeds SFT and GRPO, and, on the 8B1.7B pair, keeps improving where OPD degrades. Our analysis shows that O3PD reproduces the teachers ranking and candidate set more faithfully than OPD while departing further from its probability values, and that it allows the smallest student to move substantially further from its initialization. The order-only principle is not tied to single loss: other ranking objectives such as ListMLE also perform well. These results answer the question posed at the outset: for on-policy distillation, the teachers ordering is sufficient, and matching its probability values is not only unnecessary but can hold the student back.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: This work studies training objectives for knowledge distillation and does not involve human subjects, user data, or personally identifiable information. All experiments use publicly released models from the Qwen3 family and publicly available data: the mathematical reasoning subset of OpenThoughts for training, and the HMMT25, AIME24, and AIME25 competition problems for evaluation. We use these resources in accordance with their respective licenses and do not release any new datasets. Our experiments are restricted to mathematical reasoning, so we do not evaluate how ordinal distillation affects safety alignment or other behaviors in open-ended generation. We are not aware of any conflicts of interest related to this work.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: We have made several efforts to ensure the reproducibility of our results. The O3PD objective is fully specified in Section 3 (Equations (3) and (4)), and one training iteration is given as pseudocode in Algorithm 1. Appendix describes the experimental setup: Table 5 lists all training and evaluation hyperparameters, including the LoRA configuration, rollout length, candidate-set size, decoding parameters, and random seeds, and Figure 6 gives the exact prompt template used for both training rollouts and evaluation. The OPD baseline shares the same setup. All models (Qwen3), training data (OpenThoughts), and evaluation benchmarks (HMMT25, AIME24, AIME25) are publicly available, and our evaluation protocol (Avg@12 over three seeds, answer extraction from boxed{}) is described in Section A.

sections.title: A EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: A.1 HYPERPARAMETERS Table 5 lists the hyperparameters used for training and evaluation. We fine-tune the student with LoRA and train for 100 steps with an effective batch size of 32. During training, the teacher runs in thinking mode while the student runs in non-thinking mode, and each student rollout is limited to 1,024 tokens. At every student-generated prefix, both OPD and O3PD use the teachers top-8 candidates. For evaluation, we checkpoint every 20 steps and report Avg@12, obtained by drawing four samples per problem under each of three seeds. A.2 PROMPT TEMPLATE All training rollouts and evaluations use the same prompt, shown in Figure 6. The prompt asks the model to reason step by step and to place its final answer in boxed{}, from which we extract the answer for scoring. Prompt template Problem: {problem} Reason step by step and put the final answer in boxed{}. Figure 6: Prompt template used for training rollouts and evaluation. {problem} is replaced with the problem statement.

sections.title: B TEACHER TEMPERATURE SENSITIVITY OF OPD
sections.content: Figure 7 reports the teacher-temperature sweep. We train standard OPD for every teacherstudent pair at each {0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8} and evaluate HMMT25 Avg@12. The sweep covers the six configurations in Table 3 and additionally includes Qwen3-0.6B student. OPD is highly sensitive to , and no single temperature is best across pairs: the optimum ranges from = 0.25 (8B1.7B) to = 2 (14B8B, 4B1.7B). Sensitivity increases as the student becomes smaller. For the 0.6B student, performance collapses at high temperatures, e.g., 14B0.6B falls from 11.94 at = 1 to 1.11 at = 8. O3PD avoids this selection problem entirely, since its ranking targets are identical for every > 0. Figure 7: HMMT25 Avg@12 of standard OPD across teacherstudent pairs (rows) and teacher logit temperatures (columns). Each run is trained for only 3 steps with batch size of 32. Bold values marked with indicate the best temperature for each pair.
